title: Food Chains, Food Webs, Energy and Toxins
kicker: Cambridge Primary Checkpoint · Science 0097 · Stage 6 · Biology
summary: How to read food webs and find every food chain in them, where the energy comes from and how it passes along, and how toxic substances build up in top predators.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Read and interpret **food webs**, and find the **food chains** inside them (6Be.01)
Know that some substances are **toxic** (poisonous) and damage living things, and that they can move through a food chain or web (6Be.02)
Identify the **energy source** of a food chain or web (the Sun) and describe how energy is passed along it (6Be.03)

blocks.text: 1. Food chains

A **food chain** shows what eats what, in a line. Every food chain starts with a **producer** — a green plant (or alga) that makes its own food using **light energy** from the Sun. All the other living things in the chain are **consumers**: they get their energy by eating other living things.
Example: **grass → rabbit → fox**. The arrow means **'is eaten by'**, and it also shows the direction the **energy flows**. The arrow always points **towards the eater**.

blocks.text: 2. Food webs

In real habitats most animals eat more than one kind of food, and most are eaten by more than one predator. When food chains join together they make a **food web**. Here is a food web from farmland beside a canal.

blocks.text: **How to find every food chain in a web** — Start at a producer and follow the arrows upwards until you reach an animal with no arrow leaving it. Then go back and take every other branch. Write each chain with arrows. This web has **7** food chains:

items: grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk
grass → grasshopper → sparrow → hawk
grass → rabbit → hawk
wheat → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk
wheat → grasshopper → sparrow → hawk
wheat → mouse → snake → hawk
wheat → mouse → owl
**Producers:** grass and wheat. **Top predators:** hawk and owl (no arrows leave them).
**Herbivores** (eat only producers): rabbit, grasshopper, mouse.
The **hawk** eats three things: rabbit, sparrow and snake. The **grasshopper** is eaten by two animals: frog and sparrow.
The **longest** chains have **5** living things (for example grass → grasshopper → frog → snake → hawk).

blocks.title: Counting trick
blocks.text: To count how many food chains include one animal (for example the mouse), count the chains **into** it (wheat → mouse = 1) and multiply by the routes **out** of it to a top predator (mouse → snake → hawk, mouse → owl = 2). 1 × 2 = **2** chains.
3. What happens if one population changes?
Everything in a food web is linked, so a change in one population affects others. Use the arrows to reason one step at a time.

rows: snakes may eat **more mice**, so mice may **decrease**
the snake has lost one food, so it eats more of its other food
the mouse's only food in this web is wheat
the owl's only food in this web is the mouse

blocks.title: Use the word 'because'
blocks.text: A one-word answer ('increase') usually earns only 1 mark. For 2 marks, say what happens **and** why: 'Grasshoppers increase **because** fewer frogs are eating them.'
4. Energy in food chains

items: The **energy source** for almost every food chain is the **Sun**.
Producers (green plants) capture **light energy** and use it to make food. The energy is now stored in the plant.
When a consumer eats, the **energy stored in the food passes to the consumer**. The arrows show this transfer.

At each step, a lot of energy is **used up or lost** — for moving, for keeping warm (heat), and in waste such as droppings. Only a small part is stored in the animal's body and can pass to the next consumer.
So there is **less energy at each step** along the chain. That is why food chains are short (rarely more than 5 steps) and why there are fewer top predators than plants or herbivores.

blocks.title: بالعربي: أهم قاعدة
blocks.text: السهم في السلسلة الغذائية معناه «يتؤكل بواسطة» (is eaten by)، وبيشاور ناحية اللي بياكل، وده نفس اتجاه انتقال الطاقة. مصدر الطاقة هو الشمس (the Sun): النبات بياخد طاقة الضوء ويعمل غذاء، وبعدين الطاقة تنتقل للحيوان اللي ياكله. في كل خطوة جزء كبير من الطاقة بيضيع (حركة، حرارة، فضلات)، علشان كده الطاقة بتقل كل ما نطلع في السلسلة.
5. Toxic substances in food chains

Some substances are **toxic**: they damage or kill living things. Examples include some **pesticides** (chemicals sprayed on crops to kill insects), **heavy metals** such as mercury and lead from factory waste, and some chemicals in plastic waste.

A toxic substance can **move through a food chain**. Many of these substances stay in an animal's body instead of being broken down or passed out. A predator eats **many** prey animals during its life, so it takes in the toxin from all of them. The toxin **builds up**, and animals at the **top** of the chain often have the **largest amount** — enough to make them ill, stop their eggs hatching, or kill them.

items: A farmer sprays pesticide on wheat. A small amount stays on the plants.
Each mouse eats a lot of wheat, so each mouse takes in some pesticide.
An owl eats many mice, so it takes in the pesticide from every one of them.
The owl ends up with much more pesticide in its body than any single mouse — the owl may be harmed even though it never ate any wheat.

blocks.title: Science in your area
blocks.text: Toxic chemicals washed from farms or factories into canals and the River Nile can enter food chains: water plants → small animals → fish → fish-eating birds and people. This is why there are rules about using pesticides and about factory waste.
Worked examples
**Worked example 1** — Use the farmland food web. Write down a food chain with **four** living things that includes the sparrow. [1 mark]

items: Find the sparrow. Follow arrows down to a producer: sparrow ← grasshopper ← grass (or wheat).
Follow arrows up to the end: sparrow → hawk.
Count: grass, grasshopper, sparrow, hawk = 4.

blocks.text: **Answer:** grass → grasshopper → sparrow → hawk (or wheat → grasshopper → sparrow → hawk). **Common mistake:** arrows pointing the wrong way (hawk → sparrow). The arrow points to the eater.
**Worked example 2** — What is the source of energy for this food web? [1 mark]
**Answer:** the Sun (sunlight / light). **Common mistake:** 'grass' or 'wheat'. The producers capture the energy, but they are not its source.
**Worked example 3** — A disease kills most of the snakes. Explain what may happen to the number of frogs. [2 marks]
**Answer:** the number of frogs may increase (1) because fewer snakes are eating them (1).

**Worked example 4** — Each grasshopper in a field has 3 units of pesticide in its body. A frog eats 40 grasshoppers. A snake eats 6 such frogs. How many units of pesticide are in the snake? Assume all the pesticide stays in the animals' bodies. [2 marks]

items: Pesticide in one frog = 40 × 3 = 120 units.
Pesticide in the snake = 6 × 120 = **720 units**.

blocks.text: **Answer:** 720 units. This shows why the top consumer has the most toxin.
**Worked example 5** — Explain why energy passes from the rabbit to the fox, but not all of the rabbit's energy reaches the fox. [2 marks]

**Answer:** the fox eats the rabbit, so the energy stored in the rabbit's body passes to the fox (1). The rabbit used much of its energy for moving / keeping warm / lost it in waste, so only part is passed on (1).

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Drawing arrows from the eater to the food. Arrows go **from the food to the eater** (direction of energy).
Starting a food chain with an animal or with the Sun. Food chains start with a **producer**; the Sun is the energy source but is not written as a link in the chain.
Stopping a chain too early. Keep going until you reach an animal with no arrow leaving it.
Saying the toxin is 'made' by the top predator. It **comes from** its food and builds up.
Saying energy is 'destroyed'. Say it is **used** (for movement) or **lost** (as heat or in waste).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: **Complete** a food chain or **draw arrows** on a web — check the direction twice.
**Name** a producer, a herbivore, a predator, prey or a top predator from a web.
**Count** the food chains, or the animals that eat a named animal.
**Predict and explain** the effect of removing one population — say what happens and why (2 marks).
**Toxins**: explain why the top predator is harmed most; sometimes a simple multiplication.
**Energy**: name the source (Sun) and describe the transfer along the arrows.

questions.q: What is the source of energy for almost all food chains?
questions.e: The Sun. Green plants capture the light energy, but the Sun is the source.

questions.q: In the food chain **wheat → mouse → owl**, which living thing is the producer?
questions.e: Wheat is a green plant that makes its own food, so it is the producer.

questions.q: In a food chain, what does an arrow mean? Complete: 'is ______ by'.
questions.e: An arrow means 'is eaten by'; it points to the eater and shows the direction energy flows.

questions.q: (a) How many food chains are there in this food web?
questions.e: Grass: grass-grasshopper-frog-snake-hawk; grass-grasshopper-sparrow-hawk; grass-rabbit-hawk (3). Wheat: wheat-grasshopper-frog-snake-hawk; wheat-grasshopper-sparrow-hawk; wheat-mouse-snake-hawk; wheat-mouse-owl (4). Total 3 + 4 = 7.

questions.q: (e) All the sparrows are caught by a disease and die. Predict what will happen to the number of grasshoppers. Explain your answer.
questions.ms: 1 mark: grasshoppers increase. 1 mark: because fewer animals / no sparrows are eating them. Accept: they may later decrease again because frogs have more food and increase — only if the increase is stated first.
questions.e: The grasshoppers will increase, because the sparrows that ate them are gone (only the frogs eat them now).

questions.q: (f) The farmer sprays the wheat with a pesticide that is toxic and stays in animals' bodies. Explain why the owls may be harmed even though they do not eat wheat.
questions.ms: 1 mark: mice eat the wheat and take in the pesticide / the pesticide passes along the food chain wheat → mouse → owl. 1 mark: each owl eats many mice so the pesticide builds up / the owl gets a large amount (enough to harm it).
questions.e: Mice eat the sprayed wheat and take in the pesticide. Each owl eats many mice, so the pesticide from all of them builds up in the owl's body until there is enough to harm it.

questions.q: Each small fish in a lake contains 2 units of mercury. A large fish eats 25 small fish. A fishing bird eats 8 large fish. How many units of mercury are in the bird? (Assume all the mercury stays in the animals' bodies.)
questions.e: One large fish: 25 × 2 = 50 units. Bird: 8 × 50 = 400 units.

questions.q: Why is there less energy for the hawk than for the grasshopper in a food chain?
c: The hawk is bigger, so it needs less energy.
Energy is used or lost at every step of the chain.
The grasshopper makes its own energy.
Energy flows from the hawk down to the grasshopper.
questions.e: At each step energy is used for movement and lost as heat and in waste, so less energy reaches each later consumer.

questions.q: Describe how energy from the Sun ends up in a fox in the food chain grass → rabbit → fox.
questions.ms: 1 mark: grass (the producer) captures light energy from the Sun and stores it in the food it makes. 1 mark: the rabbit eats the grass and the fox eats the rabbit, so the (stored) energy is passed along the chain. Do not accept 'the fox gets energy from the Sun' with no chain.
questions.e: The grass uses light energy from the Sun to make food, which stores the energy. The rabbit eats the grass and gets some of that energy; the fox eats the rabbit and gets some of the rabbit's energy.

questions.q: In the chain **algae → water flea → small fish → heron**, which is the secondary consumer?
questions.e: Algae = producer; water flea = primary consumer; small fish = secondary consumer; heron = tertiary (top) consumer.

blocks.title: Remember
items: A food chain starts with a **producer**; arrows mean **'is eaten by'** and point to the eater.
A **food web** is many linked food chains — follow every branch from each producer to a top predator.
The energy source is the **Sun**; energy passes along the arrows, and some is used or lost at every step.
Removing one animal changes others: say **what** happens and **why**.
**Toxic** substances pass along food chains and build up, so top predators often get the most.
